extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of literary fiction and poetry; potential contributors to The Paris Review
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes The Paris Review's editorial mission and selection preferences: prioritizing original creative work (fiction and poetry), rejecting polemical voices, and presenting in-depth author interviews. Useful as guidance for contributors and readers about what the magazine values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize creative work (fiction and poetry) over criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Paris Review hopes to emphasize creative work—fiction and poetry—not to the exclusion of criticism, but with the aim in mind of merely removing criticism from the dominating place it holds in most literary magazines and putting it pretty much where it belongs, i.e., somewhere near the back of the book."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial aim is to prioritize original fiction and poetry above criticism; criticism may appear but should not dominate. The phrasing signals that submissions and editorial selections should foreground creative writing as the magazine's core content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Welcome "the good writers and good poets"; avoid "drumbeaters" and "axe-grinders"
rubrics_metrics.description: "I think The Paris Review should welcome these people into its pages: the good writers and good poets, the non-drumbeaters and non-axe-grinders. So long as they're good."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection favors quality of craft and voice rather than partisan, polemical, or agitational writing. The magazine seeks writers who are 'good' in literary terms and not primarily driven by repetitive slogans or combative agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on original creative work and introduction of important/emerging writers
rubrics_metrics.description: "Decade after decade, the Review has introduced the important writers of the day."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Review has a track record of publishing early or significant works by authors (examples given: Adrienne Rich; Philip Roth; V. S. Naipaul; T. Coraghessan Boyle; Jim Carroll; selections from Samuel Beckett; Jack Kerouac's short story). This suggests an openness to strong, original pieces that may mark or launch important literary careers and first appearances of significant work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let authors speak for themselves via long-form interviews (Writers at Work)
rubrics_metrics.description: "In addition to the focus on original creative work, the founding editors found another alternative to criticism—letting the authors talk about their work themselves. The Review’s Writers at Work interview series offers authors a rare opportunity to discuss their life and art at length; they have responded with some of the most revealing self-portraits in literature."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorially values in-depth, author-centered interviews that explore craft and life. The series privileges extended conversation over external criticism and has featured prominent interviewees (William Faulkner, Vladimir Nabokov, Joan Didion, Seamus Heaney, Ian McEwan, Lorrie Moore), indicating a standard for thoughtful, revealing oral/written interviews with practitioners.
